name: CANAL+
_comment_group: One more show in Static Studio. Everything that makes it a Static
Studio pack is taken from the same presets every sibling uses and is
not restated: the frame fetch, the 540x960 vertical output, the
transcription and its rewrite, the framing, the freeform text box,
the twenty characters to a line, the drag, and the margin the
caption stands on at the foot of the frame. The show asked for its
TEXT to be its own and for nothing about the pictures to change, and
that is exactly the line between this file and the presets.
What makes it CANAL+ is written in the show's own guidelines (a
three-page Canva brief), and each number below says which line of
that brief it comes from: Futura Bold, leaned and tightened, in
capitals; white; a soft drop shadow on a line set over the picture;
and a flat CANAL+ blue box, square-cornered, behind the lines picked
The id is kebab-case ASCII because it is also the folder name and
the key everything else refers to; the name is the brand, plus sign
_comment_title: The brief sets its captions as two different treatments stacked:
a line in white straight on the picture, held off it by a drop
shadow, over lines in white on a solid blue box. Both of its worked
examples open that way - 'UN JOUEUR DE D2' over 'APPELE EN EQUIPE /
DE FRANCE !', 'ET POURTANT...' over 'TOUT AVAIT SI / BIEN
COMMENCE...' - and which lines go on the blue is a decision about
the sentence, not a rule a renderer can apply: the opening beat is
one line in one caption and none in the next.
So the blue is the HIGHLIGHT, picked line by line, and the plain
treatment is the block's. A frame arrives with every line white on
the picture, and the 'Highlight Line' buttons put whichever lines
the user picks on the box. That reproduces both examples, with one
thing the renderer had to learn for it: boxes laid behind lines
that are spaced as type (see `joined` under `highlight` below).
No card. The preset's caption design is a card behind the whole
sentence, and on this show the ground is the box behind the picked
lines and nothing else, so `panel` is null. With no card there is
also no palette to offer for one, and the show's colours are fixed
by its brief anyway - white and one blue - so `colors` is left out
and no swatch rows are drawn (see `colors` in js/channels.js).
Uppercased, inherited from the preset, and stated by the brief as
well: 'Bold, italic, uppercase'.

_comment_face: Futura Bold with the brief's italic and its letter spacing of
-50 baked into the file - see content/faces/
futura-bold-oblique-canal.json for how, and for why the file
carries both rather than the renderer. The brief names the face
'Canalp'; the show supplied Futura Bold to set it in.
_comment_color: White, #FFFFFF, for every line: the brief gives the same white
for the line over the picture and for the lines on the box.
_comment_shadow: The brief's drop shadow for the line over the picture: black, an
angle of -45 (down and to the right), offset 20, blur 10,
That last number is an opacity, not a transparency, whatever the
editor calls it - its background effect on the same page is
'transparency 100' and comes out solid - so the shadow is black
The offset and the blur are the editor's own relative units and
do not convert exactly; 3px each way and a 6px blur on a 540px
still is the same soft lift the brief's screenshots show at
this size. It is the BLOCK's shadow, so it falls only on the
lines that are not on the box. A boxed line is drawn without
one, which is also what the brief does (see `highlight` below).
_comment_highlight: The brief's 'Background' effect for the lines on the blue:
Bright Blue #002DF1, corner rounding 0, fully opaque, spacing 15.
Box mode at LINE scope, overriding the preset's colour at word
scope. The brief puts whole lines on the blue and never a word
inside one, and a line-scope box is one rectangle per line, the
width of that line - so a short line has a short box, as in both
worked examples.
`joined` true, and it is what the rest of this block depends
on. The brief's boxes are its editor's 'background' effect,
laid BEHIND lines that are spaced as type at a line spacing of
1: two picked lines in a row are one blue shape stepping in
and out, and the plain opening line sits right on the blue
under it. Unjoined, a box is what its row is stacked by, and
that cannot be had - the gap between two boxes and the gap
between two plain lines are then the same `lineGap`, so boxes
that meet mean plain lines that touch. Worse, an accented
capital (the acute on an E stands 0.29em above the capitals in
this face) pushed its row down off the box above, opening a
stripe of photograph on half of all French captions. Joined,
the rows are stacked by their capitals, the boxes go behind
afterwards, and an accent overhangs into the blue above. See
`highlight.joined` in js/channels.js and joinedHighlight in
js/text.js; this is the one pack that sets it.
`padRatio` 0.17 - 8px of blue round the capitals at the size
below. The brief's spacing of 15, read the way its editor means
it, is 0.15; the extra pixel is what lets two joined boxes stay
overlapping across the slightly opened leading in `layout`
(see `lineGap` there). With the boxes joined it no longer has to
cover the accents, so it stays near the brief's number rather
than growing to hide them. A cedilla on the last picked line
hangs 3px below its box, as it would below any line.
`radius` 0 is the brief's corner rounding, stated because the
brief states it, though it is also the skeleton's own default.
The letters on the box are the block's white, and no shadow: a
boxed highlight's shadow would be the BOX's (see addBoxes in
js/text.js), and the brief's blue casts none. Null is the
preset's answer already and is not restated.
No face of its own, so the box lines are set in the block's
face and the textboxes Static Studio adds are too (see
channels.textboxFaces): the brief has one face.

_comment: The preset's block with three of the brief's numbers in it.
`fontSize` 48. The brief asks for body text between 60 and
75 in its editor's units, and both worked examples are set
at about 70 (69.7 and 71.5). Those units are not 540ths of
the frame: measured against Futura, the examples' lines fill
the frame as text of 48-49px does on a 540px still, so the
brief's canvas is about 790 units wide and its whole range
of 60-75 lands at 41-51px here. 48 is its examples. Stated
rather than fitted, for the preset's reason: forty stills
cut from one video are one set of type, not forty sizes.
The brief also asks for the second line to be larger than
the first, by up to 2 of those units - about 3%. The
renderer sets a caption at one size, and that difference is
smaller than the step between two of its pixel sizes at
this scale, so it is left out rather than faked.
`align` left, where the preset centres: every line in both
worked examples starts on one edge, and the boxes step out
to the right with the sentence.
`lineGap` 15, which is the brief's line spacing of 1 opened
by 3px. Under the joined highlight it is the leading between
capitals on every row with a box beside it: 36px of capital
in this face plus 15 is 51px baseline to baseline, against
the brief's 48 (type set solid). The brief's own 48 was
tried first and puts the acute on an E 2px INTO the line
above - the accent stands 0.29em over the capitals, and at
solid leading that is higher than the baseline it hangs
under. The brief's editor does the same, which may be why
both its examples are written without accents ('APPELE EN
EQUIPE'); a French caption here keeps them, so the leading
opens just far enough to clear them.
Between two plain lines it is measured from their ink
instead, and 15px there is close to the gap the brief's
leading leaves under a line with no accent in it. Two boxes
8px proud of their capitals across a 15px gap overlap by
1px, so they meet without a seam.
Everything else is the preset's: the width, the twenty
characters to a line, `freeform`, and the 120px the block
stands on at the foot of the frame - the examples sit about
there. The brief's 'always at least 2 lines' is what a
rewritten caption at this size comes out as on its own; it
is not something the renderer enforces.

_comment_scrim: A heavy shade thrown up from the foot of the frame, over the
photograph and under the caption. It is not written anywhere in the
brief's text, but every worked example in it has one, and it is
half of the look: the picture runs clean down to about the middle
of the frame, darkens over the next fifth, and the bottom third is
nearly black, with the photograph only just showing through it -
the legs under the shirt in the PSG example are still there, faint,
so it is not a solid fill. The caption stands in that dark band,
which is what lets plain white type with only a 30% shadow read at
all.
The numbers are read off those screenshots. `heightRatio` 0.52:
the shade starts at 48% of the frame height, where the examples'
pictures are still untouched. The stops run from the floor up -
0.9 black at the bottom edge, 0.85 at 0.6 of the span (the top of
the near-black band, about 69% down the frame), then 0.5 at 0.8
and nothing at the top. The middle stop bends the ramp, so the
fade is soft where it meets the picture and steep where it meets
the band, which is how the examples fall off; a straight line
from 0.85 to 0 showed its top edge as a line across the frame.
It is the same mechanism conspiracy-central's shade uses (see
`scrim` in js/channels.js): drawn on the canvas, not baked into
the photograph, so nothing in the image pipeline changes and the
Gradient button switches it per frame - see `branding` below.
_comment_branding: `gradient` true, and on this channel it means the SCRIM above
rather than the backend's side gradient - as on conspiracy-central
and laugh-society-snapchat. A channel with a scrim draws its own
shade on the canvas; the Gradient button (Gradient On / Gradient
Off, under the caption's frame) switches it per frame with no
round trip, and the backend is never asked for its ramp as well
On arrival, because every example in the brief has it. The button
is for the frame whose foot is already dark, or where the shade
would bury something that has to stay visible.
